characters.name: Hank Hill
characters.description: The protagonist of the show, Hank is a propane salesman who loves his job nearly as much as he loves his family. He's pretty introverted and can't cope with emotion very well, but he's clearlythe most level-headed of the cast. Abusive Parents:Downplayed, and mostly falling under this tofulfill the needs of the story or to fulfill a moral. Hank is rather emotionally controlling with Bobby and doesn't always have a good read on what his son's emotional needs are, to the point of being rather negligent. Hank continually tries to shape Bobby into being like himself, and is skeptical of allowing his son to indulge in anything he disapproves of (fantasy books, rap music, clouds on his wall, video games, and any other things that could make people see Bobby as a nerd). Some he learns to accept, others are retroactively revealed to have a justification. In theGrand Finale, Hank finally accepts his son and shows joy in what he's doing... becausehe's doing something Hank's been pressuring him to get into probably since he got into propane. In short, Hank is trying to do right by Bobby, but Hank's view of "right" is slightly myopic at times. Hank's actions atworstcould be construed as more emotional abuse, but physical abuse is one thing Hank has never, nor would ever think of. characters.name: Peggy Hill
characters.description: Peggy is Hank's wife, to whom he isHappily Married. Impulsive, egotistical, and somewhat ditzy, she sometimes causes trouble for the family with hare-brained ideas. She and Hankstay loyal to each other no matter what though. Academic Athlete: She is a former (substitute) schoolteacher with a keen interest in literature and other academic subjects, but she has taught many subjects including physical education and participates in a softball team as an adult and a teenager. She is also physically strong. Action Mom:Something she's demonstrated numerous times when it comes to defending Hank, Bobby, or Luanne. Sometimes she has to defend one from the other. To the point that she handed Leanne Platter a humiliating beat down, to successfully conning a smug con man, to shaming the Alamo Beer Company into apologizing for tainted beer, to threatening three grown men with awooden spoon. Buck Strickland is actually afraid of her.We've seen her defend Luanne from Hank, Hank from Bobby, Bobby from Hank, and Hank from Luanne. characters.name: Bobby Hill
characters.description: Bobby is Peggy and Hank's 13-year-old son, who wants to break into the entertainment business. Since he's kind of effeminate and has some strange interests (by his family's standards), Hank fears for the boy's future. He'll be all right, though. In the revival season, a now 21-year old Bobby works as the head chef of a Robata Japanese-German fusion restaurant, which he constantly struggles to keep afloat among a myriad of problems from ungrateful customers to the negligence of the Wassonasongs, who finance the establishment. While he struggles his best to balance his personal and professional lives, he's ultimately shown to have turned out all right. Acrofatic: Despite his overall lack of athletic ability, Bobby is surprisingly agile while he is "in character" for many of his comedy/mascot acts, and in season 15, despite the fact that he has largely put his comedy aside for cooking, it's shown that he has retained this ability even into adulthood. Amazingly Embarrassing Parents:Bobby feels this way at least one day of the year when Hank makes a whole birthday party for Ladybird.Peggy does this to him in the revival, largely because she keeps recounting his antics from when he was a kid to his co-workers (like how he made a twinkie smoothie when he was trying to prove himself and his cuisine to critics) Bobby feels this way at least one day of the year when Hank makes a whole birthday party for Ladybird.

characters.name: Luanne Platter
characters.description: Luanne is Peggy's niece, the daughter of her brother Hoyt. The Hills take her in early in the show's run, partially to get her away from her horrible mother Leanne. She shows a fair bit of skill in car repair during the early episodes and an ability to think for herself in a crisis at times, but is generally depicted as not being the sharpest knife in the drawer. She marries Elroy "Lucky" Kleinschmidt in "Lucky's Wedding Suit" and has a baby daughter by him named Gracie in "Monkey See, Lucky Do." Acquired Situational Narcissism: In "My Hair Lady", where she gets a job as a hair stylist at a trendy salon, and "Manger Baby Einstein", where she becomes the star of a series of direct-to-DVD children films featuring her Manger Baby puppets. Notably, every time this happens, it ends up horribly backfiring on her, either due to her getting in over her head, or becoming desperate to maintain what she has going in spite of the harm it would bring on others. Beware the Nice Ones:Despite her lack of intelligence and sometimes childish behavior, Luanne's proven to be a force to be reckoned with. Her highlights include how she handled the Hills' collective cigarette addiction, threatening Cotton for sexually harassing her, tackling an irate softball player to keep her from attacking Peggy, dealing with a trio of freeloading housemates, her competency at boxing (fighting Freeda Foreman, no less), deciding to have her baby her way rather than listen to what others want her to do, and forcing everyone to give her the wedding gifts she never received."Peggy's Pageant Fever" is a prime example of Luanne being mean on purpose. When Peggy dumps her for a professional stylist, Luanne starts nonchalantly doing things to screw with Peggy's daily routine. characters.name: Ladybird
characters.description: Hank's and the Hills' old female dog. It is no exaggeration to think Hank likes her more than Bobby or Luanne. Aging Pet Angst: Though she doesn’t die in the show's original run, her old age is frequently brought up as a source of emotional tension in some episodes, particularly for Hank. Berserk Button: Goes completely wild whenever she hears very loud noises. In a bit of aBittersweet Ending, after so much strife to keep herself from biting people around her, she finally calms down, only because she becomes deaf. Big Friendly Dog: While not exactly that big, she is portrayed as such and very rarely hurts others. The one time she was shown to be aggressive is when she is protecting the family, or, in Hank's case, reacting to his loathing of repairmen. Bus Crash: While there isno mentionof Ladybird whatsoever in season 14, it's sadly clear that she passed away at some point since she was already old at the start of the series. Season 15 shows Hank visiting her grave.

characters.name: Caesar Salad
characters.description: Aging Pet Angst: His advanced age spooks Hank, who's still hurting from the loss of Ladybird and unsure if he has it in him to endure another. Contrasting Sequel Protagonist: To Ladybird. Whereas she was a large, sturdy, and slow dog who was extremely close to Hank, Caesar is small, horrifically fragile, energetic, and is doted on more often by Peggy. Cool Old Guy: He's a capable guard dog, which is what initially causes Hank to warm up to him. Jerk with a Heart of Gold: A dog version. He's high-strung and snippy toward strangers, biting Dale when he plays an intruder and barking at Connie and Bobby before he gets to know them; but he's very affectionate to those he knows and is protective of his owners. Long List: Caesar is... not healthy. Hank was extremely put off when the medical information underneath his cage card at the adoption setup had multiple pages. To note some of the ones we're told during the episode, Caesar has: only two teeth (one after he loses it biting Dale), a bad eye, is mostly deaf, suffers from solar dermatitis, has pads so sensitive he needs to wear booties, requires frequent expression of his glands, is diabetic, suffers from anxiety and is terrified of unknown noises (despite being mostly deaf) and his own shadow. And, from the looks of how many medicines are in the cabinet, that's still barely scratching the surface.

characters.name: Cotton Hill
characters.description: Hank's father, a crotchety old man who doesn't seem to approve of anything Hank does. ThisWorld War IIvet can never stop talking about how he killed "fitty" (50) men while in service. When it comes to impulsiveness, he's even got Peggy beat. Heaven help Hank. His last appearance in the series sees him die from a horrible accident (or as he puts it,Tojofinally got him). Absurdly Elderly Father: He becomes a father for the third time in his mid-70s. Hank tries to do the math to figure out how old Cotton will be when his son G.H. is 18, but Cotton cuts him off: "I'll be dead!" Abusive Parents: Emotionally, to Hank. In "Unfortunate Son", he openly mocks Hank in front of his war buddies for being unqualified to enlist in Vietnam due to his narrow urethra. In "How to Fire a Rifle Without Really Trying", he's shown forcefully teaching Hank how to shoot a rifle... at agethree,with Cotton yelling "Close your other eye, or I'll POKE it out!!". Yeah, it's easy to see where Hank got his anger issues from. Affectionate Nickname: Calls Bobby "Bing-Bing" in response to Bobby's use of "Ging-Ging" to refer to Cotton. Artistic License – Medicine:It's pretty much impossible to sew someone's feet to their knees, as Cotton claims resulted from his war injuries. There are simply too many muscles, nerves and blood vessels in the leg and feet for that procedure to be feasible, especially given the state of medical technology in the 1940s. The closest real life procedure isrotationplasty, where a foot can be attached to the thigh but rotated 180 degrees to facilitate the wearing of a prosthetic. Michiko even expresses surprise upon meeting Cotton again that "your feet did not fall off, as predicted."The rest of Cotton's body is perfectly proportionate to his legs, even though his arms should nearly reach the ground, among other things; his design is more akin to someone of below average height (bordering on dwarfism or a similar disorder) than someone who lost their shins (or claimed to).

characters.name: Tilly Hill
characters.description: Hank's mother and Cotton Hill's first wife. Awful Wedded Life: Her marriage to Cotton was emotional hell. Cloudcuckoolander: She's certainly made some strange choices. A Day in the Limelight: "The Unbearable Blindness of Laying", "Escape From Party Island", and "The Honeymooners". Extreme Doormat: Was this throughout her marriage to Cotton.

characters.name: Didi Hill
characters.description: Cotton's 40-year-old second wife. Abusive Parents: She seems to mean well, but her absent-mindedness and general stupidity results in her often neglecting G.H., including leaving him home alone because she simply forgot about him. Blatant Lies: In Hank's view, anyway. In "The Texas Skillsaw Massacre", when Hank is accused of having anger issues (due to accidentally cutting off Dale's finder), Didi jumps on the Hank-bashing bandwagon by saying that he used to pinching the other kids when they were in kindergarten together. Hank, not really helping his case, furiously calls her a "bold-faced liar". Broken Bird: It's implied that Didi isn't happy in her marriage to Cotton but she's too meek to say anything about it. She seems confused and sad whenever she's on-screen. Candy Striper: Was one when she and Cotton first met.

characters.name: Junichiro
characters.description: Cotton's Japanese son from a fling with Michiko, and Hank's older half-brother. Appears in the "Returning Japanese" two-parter. Accidental Misnaming: Cotton can never get his name right, which continues to irritate him. The Bus Came Back: He makes a surprising return during season 14 for a lawsuit settlement on "shin jelly" Cotton used thinking that it would grow his legs back (but was actually lotion mixed with hot sauce). Calling the Old Man Out:And for good reason. He's not too pleased that his biological father decided to one day visit him, despite never being there for over fifty years of his life. He made his peace with him though. Extreme Doormat: Despite having the courage to tell off Cotton, he is submissive to the cultural norms of Japan. Hank helps him stand up for himself.

characters.name: G.H. Hill
characters.description: Cotton's infant son with Didi, which makes him Hank and Junichiro's much younger half-brother and 13-year-old Bobby's infant paternal uncle. In the revival, he is a teenager living with his single mother, who asks Hank to take G.H. under his wing as he is withdrawn and disrespectful. The Alleged Car: What he ultimately spends his settlement money on. Didi remarks that the car "looks like it has herpes." Hank tells Didi that the car is a project that he and G.H. will work on together so that he can continue to act as a good male role model for G.H. Chuck Cunningham Syndrome: After a certain point in the original series, G.H. is never seen or mentioned again, including in the final appearances on the show of both of his parents. He makes a reappearance in the 2025Hulurevival, however, now as a teenager. Deconstructed Character Archetype: G.H. is a good deconstruction of theMorality Pettrope that serves to make characters like Cotton look better despite otherwise being unlikable by design. He is less a character and more a prop and/or the result of Cotton's poor decision making and impulsivity, and as such, most of the cast don't really like him even though he has barely any agency, and he actively makes Cotton's character lookworseon principle, as his existence proves that Cotton could have been a consistently better father if he had actually tried. In fact, Cotton seems to love himtoo muchwhile never stepping up his parenting-style. Dumbass Teenage Son: By the time of the revival, G.H. is a sullen teenager who spends all of his time on social media on his phone, prompting his mother to beg his brother Hank to take him under his wing.

characters.name: Gary Kasner
characters.description: Tilly's Jewish ex-boyfriend. Alter Kocker: He's Jewish and speaks with a Yiddish accent. Bobby notices he has a funny way of speaking, and thinks it's due to being from Arizona. Beware the Nice Ones: He is normally a nice man, but as Cotton figured out the hard way, don't insult Tilly in his presence! Big Eater: He loves eating, to the point of ending up with a bypass and being prescribed a special diet that disallows most meats. He uses various excuses to get around it, such as counting chicken fried steak as "chicken" because he's allowed to have chicken, or eating seconds on Christmas because it's a special occasion. Cool Old Guy: A nice old man who gets along well with the Hills, and has a sweet relationship with Bobby.

characters.name: Michiko
characters.description: Affectionate Nickname: Cotton calls her "Ko-Ko." Defiled Forever: She had little prospects after Junichiro's birth, in part due to being a single mother, and due to Junichiro's biracial background as half American. She spent ten years living in miserable circumstances until she met Wataru. First Love: Implied with Cotton, and one can argue it's part of the reason why he treated his own wives badly, as they could never measure up to the woman he was forced to abandon. One-Shot Character: She only physically appears in "Returning Japanese Part 2," while Junichiro does make a short cameo in "Returning Japanese Part 1" Silk Hiding Steel: She might seem like an unassuming old woman, but she is the only one who gets away with making polite, yet pointed jabs at Cotton about his shins or him abandoning her.

characters.name: Chuck Garrison
characters.description: Tilly's new husband, who debuted in "The Honeymooners." Commonality Connection: He and Hank bond over their mutual love of tools, and their love for Tilly. Fourth-Date Marriage: He married Tilly after only knowing her for a few weeks. He didn't even know she was dating Gary until after they broke up, and regrets being the other man. The Loins Sleep Tonight: Tilly mentions during one of their arguments that he needs a prescription, but he retorts "not everyone's libido is the same!" It's implied to have been caused by his disapproval of their new RV lifestyle. Nice Guy: Despite Hank's paranoia, he proves to be a polite old man who enjoys hardware.

characters.name: Dusty Hill
characters.description: Yup, that one, the bassist forZZ Top. Debuted in the episode "Hank Gets Dusted" as Hank's paternal cousin. Adam Westing: He and his bandmates play fictional versions of themselves. Big Brother Bully: He acts like one to his cousin, and enjoys pranking him, although he does draw the line at involving propane. Cool Uncle: Bobby certainly thinks of him as such, and he's willing to return the affection. Everyone Has Standards: He will gladly prank Hank, but he draws the line at making fun of propane at his expense, reasoning it's going too far for a guy like him. Later, when he finds out Portis and his team were willing to mess with Hank despite his protest, he cancels his show.

characters.name: Maddy Platter
characters.description: Peggy and Hoyt's ungrateful mother and Luanne's paternal and Bobby's maternal grandmother. Arranged Marriage: Tried to get Peggy to marry a wealthy ranch owner's son, but Peggy refused, apparently leading to their ranch's future closure when their cow trail got taken over (which Peggy later averted by herself). Berserk Button: Just being around Peggy sours her mood so bad. Bus Crash: Unsurprisingly since she was already pretty old, Peggy mentions as an aside and with no gravity in season 14 that Maddy had passed in the time skip between seasons by describing her in past-tense. The Friends Who Never Hang: To date, she has never had a plot-line with her granddaughter Luanne, while in "A Rover Who Runs Through It" she essentially ignores Hank and Bobby in favor of criticizing Peggy.

characters.name: Leanne Platter
characters.description: Luanne's alcoholic, ex-con mother. Was sent to jail for stabbing her husband Hoyt (Luanne's father and Peggy's brother) with a fork. Abusive Parents: Her relationship with Luanne is shown to be negligent at best. She deprives her of attention, neglects to show up for the mother-daughter haircut at the beauty school along with Luanne’s Manger Babies puppet show, and would happily mooch off of her if she quit school and got a job. The Alcoholic: She's able to down an entire fridge of Alamo beer in just a couple of nights. And that's after rehab. Awful Wedded Life: Aside from stabbing her own husband with a fork, Hank brought up that their relationship was nothing more than "18 years of hell". Ax-Crazy: Once she goes back to drinking, she loses it. She is a violent drunk as shown by her stabbing Hoyt with a fork, being physically abusive toward Bill, and attempts to stab Buckley with a fork.

characters.name: Hoyt Platter
characters.description: Luanne's biological father (even though earlier episodes revealed that Hoyt was a wussier, male version of Peggy), Peggy Hill's older brother, and Leanne Platter's ex-husband. He was once thought to have escaped to an oil rig to get away from his abusive wife (and wouldn't come back until he got her death certificate in a fax), but a later episode revealed that this was a cover story; Hoyt was in jail and, if he screws up again, he'll be there for life. Awful Wedded Life: Leanne abused him throughout their entire marriage and Hoyt even went as far as to fool everyone into believing he left the country to get away from her and wouldn't come back unless her death certificate was faxed to him. But given she had stabbed him with a fork, it made the story all the more believable. Bitch in Sheep's Clothing: When he came back, he gave his sister Peggytwo lottery ticketsthat werealready scratched(and weren't even winning tickets). Things got worse from there until he was arrested again. Chronic Villainy: Seems incapable of passing up the opportunity to commit a crime. Daddy Had a Good Reason for Abandoning You: He's stinking in jail forever, Luanne.

characters.name: Doc Platter
characters.description: Peggy and Hoyt's father, Maddy's husband, and Luanne and Bobby's grandfather. He was never mentioned in earlier seasons, implying he had passed, but is revealed to be alive and around in his only appearance in "A Rover Runs Through It". He's presently said to have passed away by the time of the revival season. Cowboy: A wise old rural Montana cattle rancher. Early-Installment Weirdness: He was never mentioned in earlier episodes alongside Peggy's mother, implying he was deceased. However, "A Rover Runs Through It" shows he's alive and well and still with Peggy's mother. Flat Character: Doesn't have much personality outside of being a cowboy who exclusively speaks in non-sequitur dialogue. Ice-Cream Koan: He only responds with vaguely country non-sequiturs after a brief pause when asked anything. Bobby is confused while Hank finds his "cowboy talk" utterly profound, but Peggy is obviously exasperated with it from experience.

characters.name: Elroy "Lucky" Kleinschmidt
characters.description: A 35-year-old hillbilly introduced later in the series whose personal income consists primarily of nothing but personal injury suit victories. Becomes involved with Luanne, then later marries and has a child with her. Actor Allusion: In "Arlen City Bomber," Lucky says "I'm gonna help you run down that dream," an obvious reference toTom Petty's hit song "Runnin' Down a Dream." Ascended Extra: His most noteworthy scene in his debut episode ("The Redneck on Rainey Street") was when he told the story of why he was called "Lucky" (he slipped on a puddle of urine while running for the bathroom in a department store and was paid off to avoid a lawsuit), yet he was eventually elevated to main character status. His friendsElvin and Mud Dauber, more prominently featured in that episode, are converselyDemoted to Extra. Character Development: For all his faults, he has a personal code of honor, sincerely loves Luanne (and later their daughter Gracie), and does try to improve himself with Hank and Peggy's help. Chuck Cunningham Syndrome: Like his wife, Lucky doesn't appear in the revival due toTom Petty's death and his absence isn't touched on out of respect for the actor.

characters.name: Myrna Kleinschmidt
characters.description: Lucky's sister and Luanne's sister-in-law. Condescending Compassion: She does mean well, but she can be this way on occasion; at the baby shower, she takes Luanne's confusion at what a nursing pillow is, as thinking that she doesn't know she's meant tofeed her baby. Deliberately Monochrome: Her idea of decorating a baby's room was filling it with black and white decorations that it looked like they were raising a mime baby. Foil: To Peggy. They both want well for Luanne, and their future niece, but whereas Peggy relies on the old fashioned, Myrna relies on the (questionable) modern. And like Peggy, she has a tendency to overstep, as well-being as she can be. Freudian Excuse: Her trying too hard to be a modern mother stems from her squalor upbringing, where whatever food she had was roadkill. However, she has gone too far in the other direction, and her cold parenting style has turned her children into per Peggy, "book reading, water drinking robots."

characters.name: Bill Dauterive
characters.description: One of Hank's closest friends, Bill Dauterive is a Cajun Louisiana native with a promising start as a high school football player who later joined the Army with big hopes and dreams. He married someone he thought was the perfect woman, but that relationship soon went south and never looked back, and Bill found a new companion in the throes of laziness, regressed to a washed up and rotund balding man. Now middle aged, broke, and divorced, Bill's constantly depressed and full of self-loathing. The guys try to put up with him as best they can. Abhorrent Admirer: It's not subtle he has the hots for Peggy, though many of his flirtatious comments fly over Hank's head. He has no shame in watching Hank and Peggy having romantic moments... while they are supposed to be intimate inside their own house. Absurd Phobia: Of balloons,for some reason. Acquired Situational Narcissism: Occasionally when things actually go well for him. Especially when he got into bodybuilding in "Bill, Bulk and the Body Buddies". Advice Backfire:He shouldneverbe allowed nearby anybody suffering from heartbreak or having just ended a relationship, as he'll profess his own miserable life is an unavoidable outcome for them as well. Examples include Bobby, who was at peace after his mutual breakup with Connie until Bill drove him into depression by convincing him he'd already hit the high point of his life, and Kahn in the revival season, whose secret divorce had just become public knowledge.Subverted at least once, when he proved to be the only one capable of pulling Boomhauer out of a severe depression after being rejected by a woman he fell for, who ultimately turned out to be a female version of himself only looking for sex.

characters.name: Brian Robertson
characters.description: The man who rented the Hills' house during the five years Hank and Peggy were in Saudi Arabia. After the Hills move back, he continues to act as part of the gang, having grown fond of his neighbors during his time there. Black Republican: Hinted at, but inconsistently. He's aghast when Hank admits to having watched CNN but apparently had been an Obama supporter. He also voted for the extremely libertarian-leaning Dale for mayor, who ran on an anti-masking platform during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, though he also admits he only did so because he was "The Devil he knew" and didn’t even think Dale would win. The Generic Guy: So far, he doesn't have many stand-out quirks; being saner than the other guys but less neurotic than Hank. Hidden Depths: "Kahn-Scious Uncoupling" reveals Brian is a member of a Rhythm & Blues band with his friends from the barber shop he frequents. Honorary True Companion: While he no longer lives on Rainey Street, the Gang still treats him as if he does since he left a good impression during his time there. Given how he quickly grew accustomed to the group's antics, it's no wonder.

characters.name: Jeff Boomhauer
characters.description: Averyfast-talking ladies man and one of Hank's childhood friends. His dialect can be hard to keep up with, but none of his friends seem to have any trouble talking to him. The Ace: Initially portrayed as this, but his flaws become clearer later on. Even with his flaws more apparent, though, he's still an attractive, intelligent and modestly wealthy man who seems to enjoy himself on a day to day basis much more than any of his friends do. Actually Pretty Funny: Though normally unflappable, he finds his friend's jokes hilarious. Such as Dale's jokes at Hank's expense or Bill joking about them being at a gay rodeo. Ascended Extra:Downplayed, but notable. While he was always part of the main cast, season 14 has him step up to be part of more significant subplots, playing a more active role than before. Black Bead Eyes: Notably, the only main character to possess these. It lends to his normally stoic and unflappable disposition.

characters.name: Luke Jr.
characters.description: The son of Boomhauer's current girlfriend, Luke is a child prone to anxiety and generally doesn't connect well with his adult neighbors. The Generation Gap: Being one of the youngest characters in the series, he has little understanding or interest in what Boomhauer or the other adults in the neighborhood find entertaining, not being able to understand Boomhauer's speech despite having lived with him for a significant period of time. Hero Worship: He thinks Boomhauer is the coolest and wants to be just like him, despite the fact he can't understand a thing Boomhauer says. Like Father, Unlike Son: A step-parent variant; he's basically the opposite of his mom's boyfriend Boomhauer, who's go-with-the-flow, worldly, and relaxed. It ends up being beneficial for both of them; Luke Jr. learns to take more risks and overcome his anxiety to have fun, while Boomhauer learns to be a tad more conscientious than he'd been before. Both are best exemplified when Luke Jr. goes into a chicken pen to try his hand at farming, and Boomhauer immediately readies the epipen just in case. Nervous Wreck: He's noted as having social anxiety as a result of growing up during theCOVID-19 Pandemic, continuing to wear his mask long after the pandemic ended due to feeling overexposed with his full face showing.

characters.name: Patch Boomhauer
characters.description: Boomhauer's womanizing brother. Always Someone Better: He and Boomhauer always competed over everything when they were younger, and Boomhauer always came out on top; that is, except when it came to walking down the aisle. Bitch in Sheep's Clothing: He acts gentlemanly around Catherine and on the offset seems like a cool friend to the guys... but he's really a sleazebag who frequently cheats on his fiancee, and has no intention of stopping when they're finally wed. Not only that, but he is willing to throw his brother under the bus if it means hiding his infidelity. The Bus Came Back: He makes a quick cameo at Lucky and Luanne's wedding, and can be seen dancing with Meemaw Boomhauer. Dirty Coward: When Catherine catches him flirting with prostitutes at hisStag Party, he quickly hides and claims that Boomhauer was behind it.

characters.name: Dale Gribble
characters.description: Dale Gribblerounds out Hank's circle of friends. Dale, an exterminator by trade, is a paranoid conspiracy theorist who has prepared for just about any unlikely situation you can think of. And yet, he can't seem to figure out that his lovely wife Nancy is having an affair right under his nose. Act of True Love: Deconstructed. Dale worships the ground his wife walks on. When she feels insecure about her age and fading looks, Dale promises to acquire the money needed for plastic surgery by any means, even suing his beloved cigarette company. However, he performs too well, to the point of driving Nancy away. When the company, afraid of losing the case, offers him a huge settlement, he rejects it without a second thought and instead exploits an entire courtroom to reassure Nancy not only that he loves her, but he considers her the most beautiful woman in the world unconditionally. Actually Pretty Funny: Parodied. Bill will tell a joke or story but be horribly injured halfway through. Dale will refer to the joke or the story as entertaining. Afraid of Needles: To the point where he has a fit over getting his blood type test. Agent Mulder:Dale exemplifies this. Amusingly, themost obvious deceptionin his life is right in front of him.In one episode, it is revealed that he has a hugely convoluted conspiracy theory to explain this (Nancy was impregnated by an alien), which acts in many ways as the foundation for his other conspiracy theories.

characters.name: Nancy Hicks-Gribble
characters.description: Dale's wife is a reporter for a local Arlen TV station. Smarter and more responsible than Dale, she nonetheless has a 14-year affair with John Redcorn which Dale never learns about. She eventually breaks it off, but not before she gives birth to a child whom Dale is convinced is his own flesh and blood. In the revival, she is now a realtor alongside John Redcorn. Alpha Bitch: Implied to have been one (or still be one!). Just ask the weather girl before her. Most of the time she's aLovable Alpha Bitch. Ambiguous Situation:In the season 5 episode "Spin the Choice," it's vaguely implied that she told Joseph the truth about his parentage, though the season 6 episode "Of Mice and Little Green Men", where Joseph is clueless as ever, would suggest otherwise.In the revival, Nancy and John Redcorn are shown to be working together closely, but whether or not their affair has restarted is never directly addresed, only hinted at.It's not until the 15th season's episode "The Best Little Marriage In Texas" that it turns out she did restarted her affair with John Redcorn at some point. Though, she once again ends it. In the season 5 episode "Spin the Choice," it's vaguely implied that she told Joseph the truth about his parentage, though the season 6 episode "Of Mice and Little Green Men", where Joseph is clueless as ever, would suggest otherwise.

characters.name: Joseph Gribble
characters.description: Nancy Hicks-Gribble and John Redcorn's biological son, though legally the son of the former and Dale Gribble. Joseph is an awkward, dim, and horny young man who spends most of his time hanging out with Bobby. Like Dale, he has no idea that John Redcorn is his biological father. In the revival, he is now a construction worker and lives with Bobby in a Dallas apartment. Abhorrent Admirer: To Connie, who finds Joseph attractive physically but is too weirded out by his poor social skills for anything to develop between them. He has since gotten over this, since he now believes Bobby is a better fit. A Boy and His X: A boy and his horse in Season 14. Bobby purchases a horse and Joseph loves it immediately. At the end of the episode, John Redcorn promises to take the horse to his land and Joseph will come visit and ride said horse. Boys Like Creepy Critters: "The Exterminator" shows that he likes Madagascar hissing cockroaches. "King of the Ant Hill" has him (along with Bobby) collecting and keeping fire ants as pets, and various episodes have or mention him interacting with anthills in various ways.

characters.name: Bug Gribble
characters.description: The Beard: His estrangement from Dale began when Dale caught him kissing Nancy at his wedding, and Dale mistook it for him making a move on Nancy. In actuality, he was flirting with a male caterer and heard Dale coming. In his desperation to not be outed as gay, he grabbed the closest woman and kissed her, not even realizing it was Nancy until it was too late. His wife was also presumably this, and he expresses regret for stringing her along. Camp Gay: Plays up a number of stereotypically gay mannerisms, voice, and dress, in part because of his role in a gay rodeo. He even tells Hank that some of his more flamboyant mannerisms during the show are "just camp", though he's still somewhat effeminate and dramatic. Doting Parent: While early flashbacks depicted Bug as a gruff and perhaps a mean father, Bug is very loving and gentle towards Dale and glad to see him after their years of estrangement, and it's easy to see where Dale got his loving, if somewhat unorthodox, parenting style towards Joseph from. It's also important to note that these flashbacks are from the point of view ofDale, who has an established history of exaggerating and stretching the truth, even to himself. Happily Married: To Juan Pedro. He also admits that he cared about Dale's mother, but couldn't stand to continue to subject her to living with a gay man. Like Father, Like Son: In initial flashbacks, he's like a carbon copy of Dale. Even when his "true" self is revealed, he and his boy are both dramatic and theatrical.

characters.name: Bunny Hicks
characters.description: Affectionate Nickname: She calls Nancy "Sugarbear." Hair Today, Gone Tomorrow: She tells Nancy that she lost all of her hair as a result of her subconscious yearning for her former lover, Frank, and currently wears a wig. Peggy doesn't believe it, but Nancy takes her on her word. Like Father, Like Son: A female example, as much like Nancy, she had a secret affair for years, and the stress of breaking it off caused her hair to fall out. Therefore, she encourages Nancy to sleep with John Redcorn again, if at least once, if only to keep hers. "Not So Different" Remark: She uses this when she tells Nancy about her past. Southern Belle: Despite being past her prime, she is still a beautiful Southern woman who taught Nancy everything she knows.

characters.name: In General
characters.description: Always Someone Better: To the Hills. Kahn was able to get clearance on a government project while Hank works from a single-storey dealership. Minh is more glamorous and charismatic than Peggy despite being even ruder. Connie is academically gifted and an accomplished musician while Bobby tends to just follow trends. Asian Rudeness: After Cotton, Kahn and Minh are the most abrasive recurring characters and they have strong Laotian accents. Inverted with Connie who is much nicer and has an American accent. Asian Speekee Engrish: Kahn and Minh share a nonsensical, stereotypical quasi-Asian accent in the series' original run. Averted entirely by Connie in the first thirteen seasons, and by Kahn as well come season 14, though Minh isn't entirely out of the woods just yet. A Dog Named "Dog": In contrast with the Hills, they have a West Highland Terrier named Doggie. Laser-Guided Karma: For years, Kahn and Minh arrogantly mocked the Hills and their neighbors as "hillbilly rednecks" and flaunted their supposed superiority; "Khan-scious Uncoupling" revealsthey got divorced.The irony deepens when Bobby and Connie inadvertently spill the news at the anniversary party, leading to Kahn's ostracism from the Laotian community. By the end, said "hillbilly rednecks" are the only ones willing to accept Kahn after he lost everything. But with everything Kahn and Mihn put others through with their smug behavior acting like entitled jackasses, it's hard to feel sorry for them.

characters.name: Kahn Souphanousinphone
characters.description: This irritable Laotian-American systems analyst moved onto Rainey Street from Los Angeles with his wife and daughter in the series's first season. Kahn is regularly rude towards his neighbors and dismisses them as dumb rednecks. Nobody really listens to him, however, especially not his daughter, Connie. Action Dad: In "The Redneck on Rainey Street," Kahn displays significant skill as a martial artist when he gets into a fight with another redneck. This is notably the only time in the series that he actually gets into a fistfight. He almost gets into a more dangerous fight against a much,muchbigger opponent, but thankfully Hank talks him out of it. Affluent Ascetic: He's a systems analyst (and, for a brief period, was promoted to systems manager), a job that pays an average of six figures per year, yet he and his family moved to a lower middle class neighborhood. He often brags about how much wealthier he is than his neighbors, so it's possible that he did it mainly to boost his ego. All for Nothing: He spent most of his life constantly trying to gain Ted Wassanasong's approval and respect, no matter how many times he had to kiss his ass. By Season 14, their children are dating (whether or not he knew the relationship was non-monogamous is unknown, but unlikely) and Kahn hopes this means Connie will marry Chane.Once Connie and Bobby end up accidently revealing Khan and Minh's secret divorce however, Ted loses what little respect he had for Kahn, Connie herself dumps Chane after seeing how horrible he really is, and Kahn himself is shunned by the rest of the Laotian community, making all his efforts to earn Ted's approval in utter vain. Worse is even if Connie and Chane got together, Tedstillwould never show Kahn respect, since he always hated him for his obvious sucking up to him. Always Someone Better:Wantsto be this to Hank Hill and the rest of the neighbors. Hank and the others couldn't really care less as he doesn't live that much better than everyone else. Ted W

characters.name: Minh Souphanousinphone
characters.description: Kahn's wife. Just as materialistic and spiteful as him, but a smidgen more down to earth. All Girls Want Bad Boys: She chose Kahn, a rebel from a working-class background, over the boring "corporate boy" her father pushed on her. Deconstructed because while they were together for a long while, eventually Minh and Kahn divorce and Connie uses it against her when Minh tries to force Connie into a marriage with Chane. Asian Rudeness: Like Kahn, she is quite often rude to the other Rainey Street residents. Beauty, Brains, and Brawn: The brains to Nancy's beauty and Peggy's brawn. Boomerang Bigot: Not quite as much as Kahn, but she's definitely close.

characters.name: Connie Souphanousinphone
characters.description: The overachieving daughter of Kahn and Minh who is great friends with Bobby, even dating him for quite some time. A-Cup Angst: She catches Joseph staring at Luanne's bust, and promptly covers her flat chest with a forlorn look on her face. Subverted in Season 14, as by then she's a young adult and her figure has become more womanly with a sizable bust to boot.Connie:Who'd want to look at me when they could look at her? Amicable Exes: She and Bobby remain as good friends with each other after their break up and regularly hang out with each other, although there are occasional small hints she's still attracted to him.The exes part is subverted by the end of Season 14, as they officially hook up. By the end of Season 15, they're living together. Asian and Nerdy: Subverted in that while she's very smart,she would prefer to be herself instead of pursue what her father wants. That said, when she goes to college, she double majors in mechanical engineering (which is rigorous and demanding) and electrical engineering (which is extremely rigorous and absurdly demanding). Beware the Nice Ones: As nice as she is, she has little tolerance for nonsense and can become quite nasty when enraged, as Bobby often finds out.

characters.name: Buck Strickland
characters.description: Affectionate Nickname:He calls Hank “Old Top.” Bobby calls his father this in "The Buck Stops Here" when he starts copying Buck.Subverted in "That's What She Said", when Rich, a new employee, temporarily becomes Buck's new favorite because of his smutty jokes and juvenile behavior, to the extent he starts calling Rich "Old Top". He calls Hank “Old Top.” Bobby calls his father this in "The Buck Stops Here" when he starts copying Buck. Subverted in "That's What She Said", when Rich, a new employee, temporarily becomes Buck's new favorite because of his smutty jokes and juvenile behavior, to the extent he starts calling Rich "Old Top". The Alcoholic: One of his many,manyvices. All Take and No Give: With few exceptions, Buck has this relationship with Hank, constantly putting Hank through dangerous situations while refusing to reward Hank with a raise or a substantial promotion.This bites him in the ass in Season 15, when he decides to retire. Rather than give his position to Hank, who has more than earned the position as manager, Buck gives it to his bastard son Ray Roy, who knows nothing about the business and even tells Hank he's more suited as a lieutenant to clean up after Buck and now his son. This is the final straw for Hank, who realizes Buck willneverreward him for his hard work and loyalty and quits on the spot.

characters.name: Miz Liz
characters.description: The long-suffering wife of Buck Strickland. During the first half of a two-part episode, Miz Liz confronts Buck at an awards dinner while he is there with his mistress. She files for divorce from Buck and subsequently takes control of Strickland Propane. Thanks to Hank, the two end up reconciling not too long after. Bad Boss: To Debbie, at least, during her short time as owner of Strickland Propane. She demotes her husband's ex-lover to the most demeaning, degrading job at the company (tank wipe), and strives to make Debbie's life pure hell.She also uses her position to sexually harass Hank, mostly to get back at Buck. She also uses her position to sexually harass Hank, mostly to get back at Buck. Mrs. Robinson: Tries to seduce Hank in revenge for Buck cheating on her with Debbie. Hank, of course, is not interested. Silver Vixen: She's very good looking for her age.

characters.name: Joe Jack
characters.description: A coworker of Hank's, the driver of one of Strickland's propane delivery trucks, known as a "bobtail". The Alcoholic: He's got a bit of a drinking problem, usually when he gets stressed. Catchphrase: Calling anyone he talks to "Honey" regardless of gender or their relationship with him. Could also be aVerbal Ticthat doesn't imply any sexuality on his part. Disproportionate Retribution: In one episode, Buck makes the Strickland employees stay at the office overnight as a team-building exercise. While no one's exactly thrilled with the idea, Joe Jack suggestsmurderingBuck in all evident seriousness. The Dog Bites Back: Buck cruelly and abruptly fires Joe Jack (by luring him out the door, locking it behind him and screaming "you're fired!") at the beginning of "Hank Fixes Everything" as a cost-cutting measure. Later, when a fight breaks out at a propane seminar that Buck attends (and Joe Jack is working as a sandwich board guy), Joe Jack takes the opportunity to cold-cock his former boss.

characters.name: Enrique
characters.description: Hank's Mexican-American coworker. Usually a background character, but gets a fewfocus episodesin later seasons. Abhorrent Admirer: Not as bad as Bill, but he likes Hank alotmore than vice versa. Ascended Extra: Started off as a random bobtail driver. Eventually, he became a regularly appearing employee. Characterization Marches On: In earlier seasons Enrique had a more introverted personality in later seasons he's more extroverted, and social. Fun Personified: He lives for the good times, spending most of his cash on parties (and funerals). Because of this he has no savings as he blows through his paychecks.

characters.name: Debbie Grund
characters.description: One of the employees at Strickland and Buck's mistress up until Season 4when she attempts to kill Buck for calling off their affair and ends up dying instead. Abhorrent Admirer: To Hank, although it ping pongs back and forth between her being genuinely attracted to him and her just trying to get on his good side for pragmatic reasons. Ascended Extra: Started off as a minor background character before getting a larger role in "Hanky Panky". Asshole Victim:Considering how unstable she was and how she plotted to kill Buck and Liz, you can't really feel sorry for her. Bitch in Sheep's Clothing: While sleeping with a married man is a sure sign of anyone being scum, her appearance might make many dismiss her as just a clueless bimbo. Then in "Hanky Panky", she shows that she isNot Good with Rejection, to the point of attempted homicide.

characters.name: Donna (from accounting)
characters.description: A curvaceous, slightly spacey woman who works as Strickland Propane's accountant. Bunny-Ears Lawyer: Lazy and self-absorbed, but very good at web design and social networking. A Day in the Limelight: She gets her own episode where she basically signs up Strickland Propane for a very lewdMySpaceaccount which she then goes crazy with, gets herself fired, and then rehired when it becomes obvious that getting rid of her won't stop her from raising hell against Strickland on social media. The Ditz: Acts like a spacey high-schooler most of the time. Dude, Where's My Respect?: Her main motivation in "Lost inMySpace": she just wants Hank and Buck to recognize her talents rather than make her do work she's not qualified for. That she goeswayoverboard kind of negates her point. She's rehired with the compromise that they'll appreciate her work and give her more creative freedom, and in return she'll actually do the job they hired her to do.

characters.name: Roger "Booda" Sack
characters.description: A standup comedian who ends up working at Strickland Propane. Actor Allusion:Chris Rock as a provocative, motormouthed comedian?For that matter,Phil LaMarrreplacing Chris Rock, as he's also the official replacement voice forMarty the Zebra. Chris Rock as a provocative, motormouthed comedian? For that matter,Phil LaMarrreplacing Chris Rock, as he's also the official replacement voice forMarty the Zebra. The Alcoholic: Implied in "Lost inMySpace.""I was 30 days sober!"

characters.name: Tammi Duvall
characters.description: A former prostitute from Oklahoma City who was hired as the customer service representative for Strickland Propane in the episode "Ho, Yeah!". She forms a close friendship with the Hills, who allow her to temporarily stay at their place after she gets kicked out of her apartment. Hank and Peggy are unaware of her past, and the low pay at Strickland causes her to fall back into her old lifestyle, with Hank unknowingly acting as her new pimp. Book Dumb: She's a high school dropout and her eagerness to get her G.E.D. thrills Peggy to no end. '80s Hair: Has a large mane of red hair likePeg Bundy. Everyone Has Standards: Hooker or not, she turns down Buck Strickland's advances, which is one thing that Hank respects about her. Expy: She is very obviously based on Peg Bundy. He pimp is even namedAlabaster Jones.

characters.name: Melinda Grab
characters.description: A blonde, bespectacled employee of Strickland Propane who is aRecurring Extra. Amazonian Beauty: The "Lost inMySpace" episode reveals that she has six-pack abs, to the astonishment of the employees, who saw a photo of her abs online and believed them to be photoshopped. Ambiguously Gay: She hasBoyish Short Hair, six-pack abs and "Lost inMySpace" implies that she has had sex with Donna at least once. Boyish Short Hair: She has short blonde hair. Clark Kent Outfit: Melinda is usually seen wearing her Strickland uniform, so it comes as a surprise when it's revealed she has an impressive six-pack.

characters.name: Lloyd Vickers
characters.description: One of the branch managers of Strickland Propane, he owns a business degree and makes several proposals to Buck. Whilst seeming to just be a suck-up, he is ultimately placed in charge of the company when Buck suffers from a heart attack... and proceeds to screw up royally and is fired for it. Bad Boss: Takes much satisfaction in sending Hank off on the demeaning job of feeding Buck's hounds, and orders Joe Jack and the other drivers to reinstall the tattlers, or he'll gladly fire them all. He also planned on doing drug tests on the other employees for no reason. Jerkass: Once in charge of Strickland with his "fancy business degree" he quickly shows himself to be this, lording his perceived intellect on his new subordinates, gleefully putting Hank down, and outright putting tattlers in the trucks, alienating the drivers to quit. Jerkass to One: Tookspecialglee in giving Hank flex time to feed Strickland's dogs. Of course, he's still enough of an asshole to everyone else that once Hank is out of his hair, Joe Jack and the other drivers are his next target of ire. Lack of Empathy: A case that arises more from one-dimensional thinking than maliciousness, though he certainly has enough to factor it in nevertheless. Vickers thinks solely in the realm of models, such as supply-and-demand; ignoring how he was brought in to run the company through a blizzard, where many people in Arlen are in desperate need of propane. He raises the price of propane and strictly measures stopping times with tattlers, totally ignoring the real-world situation he is in.

characters.name: Ray Roy Strickland
characters.description: Affectionate Nickname: "Ray Roy" is one, as Buck couldn't be bothered to remember his name. As he tells Buck, his real name is Jody, but he doesn't care what Buck calls him. The Alcoholic: Even more so than his father. Hank actually finds him, passed out drunk in his underwear, in the manager's office at Strickland Propane. From dialogue earlier in this scene, Hank also suggests that Ray Roy may have been so drunk that he wet himself. The Ditz: Ray Roy used propane to inflate balloons at a children's party according to Peggy, he believes Hank's lie that blood is half the weight per gallon of propane, caused Strickland North to go "tits up," is so bad at running Strickland Propane that the company is on Death's door by the time Hank comes back, and fails to maintain its office building. Epic Fail: Ray Roy's leadership of Strickland Propane in general. Not only is it on the brink of ruin by the time Hank comes back, but the building is an absolute mess, with vandalized signage, blatant code violations like an open storage locker, garbage and urine littering the sales floor, and a trashed manager's office.This is what triggers Hank to buy 51% of the company.It's a good wonder Joe Jack, Roger and Enrique stuck it out despite all that. Like Father, Like Son: Despite only meeting his father once, he shares his bottomless appetite for women, alcohol and his love of propane. To this end, he opened his own propane dealership - also called Strickland Propane - in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, and used most of Buck's slogan in the process. He also knows Buck's plan of a "first class hospitality suite" without his father explaining it to him. This is portrayed as a very bad thing when they finally meet each other; they end up bringing out the worst in each other and Ray Roy even says that their similarities are probably the reason his mother never wanted them to meet.

characters.name: Ted Wassonasong
characters.description: Wealthy Laotian businessman, and object of Kahn's borderline worship. He is the main investor in Robata Chane, a restaurant operated nominally by his son Chane, and functionally by Bobby. The Ace: He's a rich, successful business owner. Affably Evil: He's polite and charming, but he's always the main antagonist in his appearances. He might not be so bad if he wasn't such a greedy, self-centered jerk. Broken Pedestal: Ted becomes one to Kahn after the events of "Orange You Sad I Did Say Banana." Kahn idolized Ted up to that point in the show (at least in the sense he wanted to be as successful as him), but that episode made Kahn lose respect for him after realizing he shouldn't let someone else tell him or his family how to live.It doesn't last. Catchphrase: "Super nice!"

characters.name: Chane Wassonasong
characters.description: Ted and Cindy's teenaged son, an overachieving, insufferableJerkasswho enjoys tormenting Bobby and pursuing the decidedly uninterested Connie. In season 14, as an adult, he is a co-owner and the namesake of Robata Chane, the Dallas restaurant where Bobby is the executive chef, though Chane himself does little-to-nothing to actually run it. Abhorrent Admirer: To Connie, who considers him "a boring know-at-all who talks about himself and cheats at miniature golf." Not helped by Kahn and Minh constantly pushing Chane on her. All Take and No Give: A key aspect of his character in the revival. Despite positioning himself as the co-owner of Robata-Chane, it's made clear that he does nothing to actually run the establishment, delegating all the work onto Bobby and his subordinates while Chane spends all his time partying with his friends and womanizing. He likewise seems to value his relationship with Connie entirely on the basis of what she gives him (namely the approval of his parents), and it's strongly implied the entire reason why he pursued an open relationship with her was so that he wouldn't have to emotionally commit.Sure enough, when Connie is left distraught following the outing of her parents' divorce, Chane shows his more odious colors when he complains about having to pay attention to her "feelings" and wanting to keep to just having sex with her, prompting Connie to break up with him. Always Someone Better: Connie is this for him. He (as well as Connie's parents) try to impress her with his achievements only for Connie to rebut that she's excelled better than Chane in the same fields. Examples being Kahn telling Connie that Chane is a second chair oboe and won second place in the science fair. Connie reminds him that she'sfirstchair violin and wonfirstprize in that same science fair. Ascended Extra: After appearing in only eight episodes of the original run, Chane becomes a much more important part of the 2025 revival.

characters.name: Laoma Souphanousinphone
characters.description: Catchphrase: "If I may just demonstrate?" May–December Romance: Starts a romantic relationship with Bill, who is middle aged, and her son's neighbor. Obnoxious In-Laws: To Minh, always feeling the need to show her how to cook and clean. Minh was reluctant to help Peggy with her column in "Bystand Me" because it meant calling Laoma. Old Maid: As Dale puts it, she literally is one, being an older, widowed woman who works as a maid to get out of the house. Put on a Bus: Because "Maid in Arlen" aired when King of the Hill was beginning to be syndicated, her plotline with Bill was abruptly ended without any measure of finality. She was mentioned on the phone during "Bystand Me" with Peggy using her tips to write a household hints column. Sadly, season 14 confirms thatLaoma passed awaywith Kahn saying he never forgave Bill for dating his late mother.

characters.name: Tid Pao Souphanousinphone
characters.description: All Girls Want Bad Boys: She's the receiving end of a gender inverted version of this trope. Bobby falls for her because she's a tough city girl from LA. City Mouse: A drug dealer from LA who doesn't take the quiet life in rural Texas well. City People Eat Sushi: Bobby takes her to a sushi restaurant on their date to seem "cool" but she can tell from one bite that the tuna came from a can. Cool and Unusual Punishment: Forced to stay in Arlen to keep her out of trouble after stealing drugs from a street gang and planned to fly back to LA on her own once she got enough money to pay off her debt. GoesFrom Bad to Worsewhen she's caught and sent to live with another one of Kahn's brothers who's a cattle rancher in the Midwest. Her uncle warns her that if she screws up again, he'll send her to live with her grandmother in Laos, then puts her to work shoveling manure. Even Evil Has Standards: Upon being introduced in class, she doesn't take it well when the teacher makes various mocking nicknames out of her name, and her face visibly shrinks. It could subtly implied that she was insecure and has dealt with racism back in LA. Downplayed, as it doesn't stop her from treating Bobby like a stupid hick or calling him a pig farmer.

characters.name: Principal Moss
characters.description: The Alcoholic: A functional alcoholic, but an alcoholic nonetheless.Moss:"I have that disease where you wake up in strange places drunk." Apathetic Teacher: The Principal version. He's mostly trying to get by doing as little work as possible while swiping whatever bonus he could. He couldn't care less about the students' performance if he tried, unless it involves him possibly losing his job. Deadpan Snarker: Years in the education system will do that to you. Dirty Coward: Next to his apathy for his students, cowardice is Moss's defining characteristic. He once fakes a heart attack to avoid casting the deciding vote at a PTA meeting; a potential riot and a miffed-looking Hank send him scrambling for the emergency exit on other occasions. Everyone Has Standards: Even the morally dodgy Moss is appalled by Bobby's rash of testicle kicking.

characters.name: Officer Brown
characters.description: A recurring character in later seasons, an Arlen police officer noted for his laziness and corruption. Dirty Cop: He openly takes bribes from Buck in "Trans-Fascism" and is mentioned as tampering with evidence is one episode. Ink-Suit Actor: Looks like Fred Willard. Jaded Washout: Says Principal Moss: "Officer Brown may be a disgraced cop who tampered with evidence, but this here used to be a man." Officer Brown doesn't disagree. Knight Templar: He's eager to see "action," even when there's none to be had. He once tries to shoot Ladybird during a thunderstorm, (after she's been reported as a dangerous dog). He's also a bit too enthusiastic in helping Bobby track down truant Clark Peters and Dooley, though, in fairness, he's beenReassigned to Antarcticaand hasn't done real police work in a while.

characters.name: Coach Sauers
characters.description: Arlen High's former football coach who led the school's football team (including Hank, Bill, and Boomhauer) to the Texas State Championship, which they lost. He's later brought back to coach Bobby's Tom Landry Middle School football team. Broken Pedestal: Hank looked up to Coach Sauers as he led Arlen High to the state championship, which Hank looks at him fondly, despite losing at the end. But when he discovers Sauers chasing the boys around the field with his car, he instantly loses all respect for him and bashes him in the head with a water cooler to stop him. Peggy notes to Hank that Hank used to have this opinion of him when Hank was a student, but enough time has passed that Hank applied aNostalgia Filterand only remembered the games they won with him rather than his gruesome training methods. Drill Sergeant Nasty: While Hank and the Arlen High alumni hold him in high regard,his techniques to "toughen up" and motivate the players end up scaring away Bobby, Joseph and the rest of the team. Even Hank is appalled with how far he goes.It should be noted that while Hank seems to have forgotten this about him at first, Peggy remembers how much Hank hated this aspect of Coach Sauers. Fallen-on-Hard-Times Job: When Hank decides to seek out Sauers to offer him a coaching job, he wonders where he ended up. The scene then cuts to Sauers standing in front of a crowded stadium, implying he's coaching for a professional team.The camera then zooms out revealing the stadium to just be a decorative backdrop at the sporting goods store he works at. Foil: He's one to the Soccer Coach Lucas. While Sauers is passionate about winning the game and uses extreme methods to attempt to whip the team into shape, Lucas praises his players for practically doing nothing and doesn't seem to particularly mind if they win or lose. Arguably to Hank, as well. He offers a more extreme version of Hank's obsession with sports and masculinity, and he completely lacks Hank's moral compass and empathy

characters.name: Coach Kleehammer
characters.description: Tom Landry Middle School's obnoxious, somewhat dimwitted gym teacher and wrestling coach, a recurring character in Bobby-centered stories. Very similar to Coach Sauer, but lacks that character's outright psychotic edge. Book Dumb: Not only is he unintelligent but seems to hold "book-learning" and other teachers in contempt. In one episode, he's briefly made Principal and spends the whole time yelling at students."Study up today, maggots!" Jerk Jock: The "washed-up coach" variety. Last-Name Basis: We never learn his given name. He also refers to most students by their last name, and even does it to Hank and Dale when he helps them with flag football training. Malaproper: "It's all about you boys and your tomfooligans!"

characters.name: Emily
characters.description: Tom Landry Middle School's no-nonsense 13-year-old hall monitor The Dragon: She is Principal Moss's main enforcer, Her duties range from escorting recently terminated employees off of school property to ensuring that the morning student announcement is up to acceptable standards. Phrase Catcher: Whenever Principal Moss yells "EM-LAY!", you know some serious business is about to go down at Landry Middle School. Police Brutality: Essentially the school resource officer, despite her young age, Emily is not above using physical force to carry out her duties. Yellow Sash of Power: Orange vest in this case. She takes her jobveryseriously. In fact, she is vested with authority well beyond the scope of a hall monitor. With most of Landry's adult faculty, Moss included, being rather timid bureaucrats who claim their hands are tied by regulations, Emily is one of the few real authority figures in the school.

characters.name: Clark Peters
characters.description: A fat bully with a weird haircut, and seemingly perpetual stuffy nose. '80s Hair: He shave the sides of his head and grows the rest of his hair long, making a mullet. The Bully: Constantly picks on Bobby and occasionally forces him to do his homework for him. Creepy Child:Implied.As his teacher remarked, "The Clark Peters I know likes to burn things".Mihn also once referred to him as "that creepy booger-nosed kid". As his teacher remarked, "The Clark Peters I know likes to burn things".

characters.name: Dooley
characters.description: The monosyllabic bad teen at Tom Landry Middle School. Brutal Honesty: When he's not pointing out the obvious, he makes very blunt statements with no regard for whether what he says will upset the listener. The Bully: The most consistent one, right next to Clark. Captain Obvious: The majority of his dialogue consists of pointing out the obvious. Creepy Monotone: He also has a very deep voice for a teen in middle school.

characters.name: Marie
characters.description: The school's hall monitor. She's a strict vegetarian who ends up being charmed by Bobby's humor and his "first" girlfriend. Bitch in Sheep's Clothing:Downplayed. While she's aNice Girl, Marie demonstrates that she doesn't really tolerate other people with views that contradict her own, like Bobby wanting to eat meat, and somewhat led him on thinking they're a couple after kissing on the lips. First Love:Subverted. Despite Bobby believing that they become "boyfriend-girlfriend" after kissing, it's clear that Marie doesn't see it that way. Jerkass Has a Point: While yes, Marie was a bit harsh with Bobby and did lead him on somewhat, he did arguably overreact to her dancing with other guys (especially since there was no real agreement between the two that she would only spend time with Bobby and no other guys) at the party with him making a big scene in front of everyone instead of simply calmly asking her about it, so you can't really blame her too much for being off-put by Bobby being overly clingy and jealous and wanting to distance herself from him. Platonic Kissing: Marie gives Bobby one right on the lips (something she apparently does with her friends regularly). While it's not a big deal to Marie, Bobby takes it as a romantic gesture, leading him to think Marie's his girlfriend.

characters.name: Lenore Dauterive
characters.description: Bill's ex-wife who was very unfaithful to him during their marriage before dumping him for good. She briefly returns back to Bill while he's going out with former Texas governor Ann Richards. Awful Wedded Life: From what little is known about their marriage, it's been said to be turbulent. Bill wasExiled to the Couchon their honeymoon and their marriage consisted of them fighting so loud, all the neighbors could hear every hour of the day, and Lenore sleeping around with other people. Bitch in Sheep's Clothing: Lenore returns back to Bill's life after all these years and seems interested in rekindling their relationship. After Bill's relationship ends with the latter, the former seems flattered he ended the relationship with Ann Richards for her. But after Bill asks Lenore to marry him again, she turns him down and doesn't even tell him where she's living now. And her playing it up to Ann Richards over how Bill proposed to her shows him she only came back because of all the attention he's been getting from Ann Richards. The Ghost: She was mentioned in the first few seasons, talking about how her and Bill'sAwful Wedded Lifebefore leaving him. Green-Eyed Epiphany: Subverted. Lenore returns back to Bill's life, seemingly into him again. But it's only because of the attention he's received for going out with Ann Richards. And when Bill proposes to Lenore during his birthday party, she declines and doesn't even tell him where she's living now. But the moment Ann Richards briefly drops by, Lenore plays it up, saying how Bill asked her to marry him. And when Bill briefly goes into Ann Richards' limo, Richards and Bill have a talk about how he shouldn't go back to her, all while a jealous Lenore screams at him to get out of the limo and marry her. In the end, Lenore is just using Bill for her advantage without having any feelings for him whatsoever.

characters.name: Gilbert Dautrieve
characters.description: Bill's cousin who still lives in Louisiana. Abhorrent Admirer: To Hank of theIncompatible Orientationtype. He's very clearly attracted to Hank and hits on him several times, much to Hank's discomfort. Blue-and-Orange Morality: The most charitable way to consider Gilbert's differing thought process on him selling the family land compared to Bill attempting to franchise the family sauce recipe in an attempt to follow his cousin's example. To Gilbert, he was forced to sacrifice their heritage in a way for their name to live on, whereas Bill apparently just sold out one of their treasured family secrets for the sake of money. In his mind, physical things like property are things that, while painful to part with, are acceptable to sacrifice for "honor", but actual family secrets and traditionsmustremain within the Dauterive bloodline. Camp Gay: Albeit with aSouthern Gentlemanvibe. The Dandy: Finely dressed and always willing to dispense advice on how to become aSouthern Gentleman. His mentoring of Bobby in this regard is played completely seriously and he at no point mocks Bobby.

characters.name: Lily, Rose, and Violetta Dauterive
characters.description: Bill's cousins (Lily and Rose by marriage, Violetta by blood). As their husbands died in their 20s, they seek to marry Bill to pass the Dauterive name onto the next generation. Ambiguously Related: It's never stated if Violetta and Gilbert are siblings or cousins, although based on Aunt Esme's wording, Violetta is her daughter. Bitch in Sheep's Clothing: Violetta seems perfectly polite and proper, but after Bill turns down her advances, she lies to Aunt Esme and says that she discovered Lily, Bill and Rose in the throes of passion. It's enough for Bill to be kicked out of the estate. Cat Fight: All three engage in one that's so titillating it's outright hilarious. Chosen Conception Partner: The three of them want to sleep with Bill because he's the last remaining Dauterive besides Gilbert, and therefore, he can give them children and continue the family line, but they do seem to be enchanted by him otherwise.

characters.name: Esme Dauterive
characters.description: Bill's aunt, who wants to help continue the Dauterive family line. Get Out!: She forces Bill to leave when he says that he isn't at the Dauterive mansion to "till the soil" ie sire children, but "play in the garden" and sleep with the girls. The Ghost: Not her, but possibly her husband, Bill's blood uncle Alphonse. Peggy believes he's deceased, but Esme says that he "lingers in a room in the back of the house" hoping to see the Dauterive name passed on to another generation. In any case, he's dead by "Blood and Sauce." Gratuitous French: Courtesy of being voiced by Meryl Streep, she can speak fluent Creole, and often holds long conversations with Bill in it. I Want Grandkids: Well, more like niblings in Bill's case, but she and her husband Alphonse hope to see the Dauterive name passed onto another generation. The problem is her sons or sons-in-law are dead, Gilbert is implied to be gay, and Bill is an unhappily divorced loser. She was willing to let Bill stay with them, provided he "till the soil" and have children with her daughters-in-law, but throws him out when he admits that isn't the case.

characters.name: Lane Pratley
characters.description: A crooked car dealer who owns several dealerships in Arlen. Bad Boss: He horribly mistreats and underpays his women's roller derby team in "Arlen City Bomber." Dirty Old Man: In "Ho Yeah!", it's implied he patronized Tammi Duvall's services. He also joins Luanne's Bible class in her pool so he could ogle at her in "The Good Buck." Family Business: His father is also a car dealer. In "Nine Pretty Darn Angry Men" Lane remarks that he plans on taking over his dad's dealership when he passes. Honest John's Dealership: A corrupt but charismatic car dealer who tends to talk his customers into paying extra for his wares. He also fits the look as a sly salesman with his tacky suits and shit-eating grin.

characters.name: Chuck Mangione
characters.description: Spokesman for the Mega-Lo-Mart, frequently seen around Heimlich County. Adam Westing: He evidently has anger management problems, as he shows up in the same anger-management class Hank is forced into in "The Texas Skillsaw Massacre"... and evidently learned very little from it, as he whacks the teacher upside the head with his fugelhorn just for spelling his name wrong.Despite the fact the teacher had done that as a final test that he did with Hank first in front of the whole class.One majorRunning Gagabout him is also how the only song anybody knows about him (and, in turn, the only songheknows how to play) is "Feels So Good".noteWorth nothing that Mangione wasn'tquitea one-hit wonder inReal Life; he scored a second Top 40 hit with "Give It All You Got," which he composed as the theme song for the 1980 Winter Olympics, and his soundtrack forChildren of Sanchezwent Gold even though it scored no Top 40 singles. As Himself: Started out as Mega-Lo-Mart's spokesman, before apparently relocating to Arlen permanently (after living in the Megalomart). Berserk Button: Either spelling his name wrong or calling him a chick. Possibly the reason why he wasin an anger management class. The Ditz: He was in anger management class and could have passed if it wasn't for the fact he failed the misspelled name test despite seeing Hank going through itright in front of Chuck.

characters.name: M.F. Thatherton
characters.description: Former Strickland Propane employee, now Buck's business opponent and mortal enemy. Evil Counterpart: He is Strickland's according to Hank. In reality, they're not that different. His business, Thatherton Fuels, is a better example being an evil counterpart to Strickland Propane as they rely heavily on cutting corners and gimmicky marketing tactics towards gaining sales compared to Strickland Propane's focus on quality customer service. Foil: He is one to Hank, who believes in giving honest goods and quality service to the customer, where Thatherton only cares about getting the money and has no problem cutting corners. This is explained quite well in a flashback in Thatherton’s debut episode where Thatherton still worked for Buck. Hank is loyal to Strickland and wants to give the customers honest goods and quality service. Thatherton says he’s making his own business and got Buck’s top three accounts already interested in working with him. Go-Karting with Bowser: Often plays cards and gambles with his rival Buck Strickland. Hidden Depths: "Lost in Myspace" shows that he's a huge fan of the bandWeezer.

characters.name: Anthony Page
characters.description: A government employee originally from Los Angeles who has appeared as both a social worker and a legal advisor for civil rights cases. He has attempted to get Bobby taken away from Hank, falsely believing Hank to be an abusive father, and also enforce an ill-advised policy that would force Strickland Propane to accept drug addiction as a disability. He is probably the closest thingKing of the Hillhas to a recurring villain. The Alleged Expert: One of many,manypeople who get on Hank's nerves because they do their assigned work without an ounce of common sense. He doesn't even follow up on the claim that Bobby's black eye came from getting hit with a baseball by talking to Bobby's Little League coach. When his boss asks him specifically about that, all Anthony can do is give some embarrassedMirthless Laughter. Condescending Compassion: He derides the Hills and their neighbors as "Redneck City", and it's implied that he thinks removing Bobby from Hank and Peggy's care will "save" him from his community's "redneck" values. Forgotten First Meeting: In “Junkie Business”, no mention is made of Hank and Anthony’s first meeting. In a DVD extra, Hank does refer to Anthony as “Twig Boy!” and it can be implied by the episode that Anthony is using Leon to get back at Hank, it can also be seen as Anthony just being used to be a villain. Hate Sink: He's a brash, uncaring bureaucrat who looks down on Arlen's residents, especially Hank. Each of his appearances has him abusing his power to get what he wants if it means Hank will be miserable.

characters.name: Jimmy Wichard
characters.description: A not-too-bright man who works at the local racetrack. According to Dale, he fried his brain while staring at the sun too long, which also suggests that he was pretty stupid to begin with for doing that in the first place. Bad Boss:Puts Bobby's life in danger bytrying to make him cross a racetrackduring a car raceto bring him a soda.When Hank is considering going to work for Thatherton Fuels in the flashback in "Propane Recall", Jimmy barges into the room and immediately starts screaming at Hank for threatening being his "Number 2" and trying to assert dominance over him.Hank bails immediately because of thiswith Jimmy screaming at him for posting the "help wanted" sign back up, showing he had, if anything, become even more abusive. Puts Bobby's life in danger bytrying to make him cross a racetrackduring a car raceto bring him a soda. When Hank is considering going to work for Thatherton Fuels in the flashback in "Propane Recall", Jimmy barges into the room and immediately starts screaming at Hank for threatening being his "Number 2" and trying to assert dominance over him.Hank bails immediately because of thiswith Jimmy screaming at him for posting the "help wanted" sign back up, showing he had, if anything, become even more abusive. The Bully: Whoever has the misfortune of working for him better be prepared to deal with scut jobs and verbal abuse.

characters.name: Reverend Stroup
characters.description: The pastor of Arlen First Methodist Church, who is originally from St. Paul, Minnesota. All Love Is Unrequited: Has a long-standing crush on Bill. They eventually date in "Passion of the Dautrieve," butit doesn't work outdue to Bill liking the romance when it was "forbidden" rather than when she quit her job as pastor to make it normal. Beware the Nice Ones: Judging from her breakup with Bill:Peggy:"I always pictured her as a crier, not a screamer."She also doesn’t really humor Hank’s complaints about his seat being “stolen”, tearing down the argument and leaving him feeling defeated. She also doesn’t really humor Hank’s complaints about his seat being “stolen”, tearing down the argument and leaving him feeling defeated. Comically Missing the Point: Has a tendency towards this.

characters.name: Chris Sizemore
characters.description: Peggy's boss at Sizemore Realty. Affably Evil: He rarely drops that smarmy smile, but he's definitely not a nice man. Bitch in Sheep's Clothing: On the surface, he's a generous and respectable businessman. In reality, he's a narcissistic, petty, vindictive old cheat. Hidden Depths: Is a passionate actor, as evidenced in "Six Characters in Search of a House". Ink-Suit Actor: Looks a lot like his voice actor.

characters.name: Bob Jenkins
characters.description: One of Peggy's coworkers at theArlen Bystander, a crusty, one-eyed veteran reporter with a sarcastic sense of humor. He appears a few times after Peggy leaves theBystander. The Alcoholic: By his own admission.It doesn't seem to affect his character much. Deadpan Snarker: Sardonic comments are like a second language for him. Eyepatch of Power: He got it from brain tumor surgery. Gallows Humor: Jokes about losing his eye when the editor threw a story back in his face.

characters.name: Eli Selwick
